cards.title: Naming your emotions: The feelings wheel
facts: Psychologist Dan Siegel coined 'Name it to tame it': labeling an emotion activates the brain's prefrontal cortex, reducing amygdala reactivity.
Vague labels like 'bad' or 'weird' keep distress fuzzy; identifying 'lonely', 'overwhelmed', or 'envious' leads to targeted solutions.
do: Use an emotion wheel or mood chart to identify the precise sub-emotion you are experiencing
Acknowledge feelings without judgment: 'I am noticing a sensation of envy in my chest'
Remember that emotions are temporary brain signals, not permanent personal identities
dont: Never suppress or bottle up painful feelings hoping they will magically vanish
Never shame yourself for experiencing normal human feelings like jealousy or fear

myths.statement: Mentally strong people never feel sad, anxious, jealous, or overwhelmed.
myths.truth: Emotional strength is not feeling numb; it is having the self-awareness to recognize painful emotions and process them healthily.

quiz.q: What happens in your brain when you accurately name a strong, distressing emotion?
options: Your brain shuts down completely
The logical prefrontal cortex activates, helping calm down the amygdala alarm center
Your heart rate doubles instantly
Emotions get permanently stuck in your head
quiz.explanation: Labeling emotions ('naming to tame') dampens autonomic nervous arousal and restores cognitive clarity.

situations: After receiving lower marks than expected at {at}, {name} feels a tight heaviness in their stomach and snaps angrily at a sibling.
scenario.question: How should {name} process this emotional state constructively?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Pause and identify the underlying emotion: disappointment and embarrassment rather than pure anger
rubric.keys: name disappointment|underlying emotion|name it to tame it

rubric.point: Acknowledge that feeling sad or disappointed after hard work is completely valid and normal
Apologize to the sibling and take three slow, calming breaths
rubric.note: Takes relational responsibility and resets physiology.

dangerous: bottle up emotions and pretend everything is perfect

sources.name: National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS)

cards.title: Taming exam anxiety: The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique
facts: Exam anxiety triggers a fight-or-flight adrenal surge that reduces working memory and makes your mind feel blank.
Physical grounding (5-4-3-2-1 sensory check) and 4-7-8 rhythmic breathing physically downshift the nervous system within 90 seconds.
do: Practice 5-4-3-2-1: Name 5 things you see, 4 things you can touch, 3 sounds you hear, 2 things you smell, 1 thing you taste
Inhale through your nose for 4 seconds, hold for 7 seconds, exhale slowly through pursed lips for 8 seconds
Remind yourself: 'An exam measures my preparation on a few questions today, not my entire worth as a human'
dont: Never hyperventilate with shallow chest breathing when panic surges
Never stay up all night drinking caffeine before a morning examination

myths.statement: If your mind goes blank in an exam hall, it means you have forgotten everything and are doomed to fail.
myths.truth: A blank mind is temporary cortisol-induced working memory vasoconstriction. Calming your breath restores memory access within 2 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the immediate physiological goal of using the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique?
options: To memorize 5 math formulas simultaneously
To pull sensory attention back into the present moment and deactivate the fight-or-flight panic cycle
To fall into deep sleep during the test
To test your eyesight
quiz.explanation: Grounding breaks catastrophic mental loops by reconnecting your attention with immediate physical reality.

situations: Inside the exam hall at {at}, {name} flips open the question paper, feels their heart hammering at 140 bpm, and feels completely blank.
scenario.question: What should {name} do in the first 2 minutes?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Put the pen down, close eyes, and take three deliberate 4-7-8 slow breaths into the belly
Use the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique to reconnect with the physical desk and surroundings
rubric.note: Deactivates panic cascade through present-moment sensory focus.

rubric.point: Scan the paper for the single easiest question you recognize and solve that first to rebuild momentum
rubric.note: Restores cognitive confidence through small wins.

dangerous: run out of the hall screaming
give up and leave paper blank

cards.title: Saying 'No' with kindness: Healthy boundaries protect you
facts: Saying 'yes' to everyone else often means saying 'no' to your own mental health, sleep, and core duties.
A boundary is not an attack or rejection of the other person; it is a clear statement of what you can and cannot do.
do: Use clear, polite phrases: 'I can't take that on right now, but thank you for thinking of me'
Deliver your refusal without long, fabricated excuses; simple clarity commands respect
Notice if you say 'yes' purely out of fear that people will stop liking you
dont: Never apologize excessively for protecting your study hours or rest
Never agree to do a classmate's homework out of fear of being cast out of the group

myths.statement: Being a kind and caring friend means you must agree to every single request anyone asks of you.
myths.truth: Compulsive agreeableness is people-pleasing, not kindness. Healthy relationships require mutual boundaries and honest limits.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the most mature way to decline an unmanageable favor from a friend?
options: Make up an elaborate lie about a fake doctor appointment
State calmly: 'I'd love to help, but I'm booked with exam revision this evening, so I can't join'
Ignore their calls for three weeks
Yell at them for being selfish
quiz.explanation: Honest, prompt, and calm boundaries preserve self-respect and friendship without deception.

situations: A popular classmate at {at} demands that {name} write their complete history essay project by tomorrow morning.
scenario.question: How should {name} assert this personal boundary?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Say clearly and calmly: 'No, I cannot write your project for you, but I can share the library book links'
rubric.note: Sets a firm ethical boundary with helpful alternative.
rubric.keys: refuse to write essay|say no clearly|set firm boundary

rubric.point: Recognize that true friendship is never conditional on completing someone else's academic work
rubric.keys: friendship not conditional on homework|reject pressure

rubric.point: Seek advice from a teacher or parent if the classmate uses bullying or threats
rubric.note: Escalates extortion safely to trusted adults.
rubric.keys: tell teacher if threatened|seek adult support

dangerous: stay up all night writing peer's essay

sources.name: NIMHANS Child & Adolescent Mental Health Services

cards.title: The 4-part genuine apology: Repairing damaged trust
facts: A fake apology says 'I am sorry IF you felt hurt'; a genuine apology takes full ownership: 'I was wrong, I hurt you, and I will fix it.'
The four parts of an authentic apology: Own the specific action, Acknowledge the impact, Make amends, and Change the behavior.
do: Say explicitly: 'I was wrong to share your secret; I broke your trust and made you feel exposed'
Ask sincerely: 'What can I do to help make this right between us?'
Give the hurt person space and time to forgive you without demanding immediate smiles
dont: Never attach defensive justifications: 'I am sorry, BUT you provoked me first'
Never expect someone to trust you instantly just because you said the word 'sorry'

myths.statement: Adding the word 'BUT' in an apology ('I'm sorry, BUT you started it') makes the apology more balanced and fair.
myths.truth: Using 'but' instantly cancels out the apology, shifting blame back onto the victim and deepening emotional damage.

quiz.q: What makes an apology genuinely restorative and mature?
options: Blaming someone else for your actions
Taking clear responsibility for specific harm, expressing remorse, and offering concrete restitution
Buying expensive candy to bribe them
Posting a vague status on social media
quiz.explanation: Authentic apologies focus entirely on acknowledging harm, taking responsibility, and changing future conduct.

situations: In the school corridor at {at}, {name} repeated a humiliating rumor about a friend to get laughs from a group of classmates.
scenario.question: How should {name} deliver a sincere restorative apology?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Approach the friend privately and take unconditional ownership of the betrayal without excuses
Acknowledge the specific emotional hurt and humiliation caused by repeating the rumor
rubric.note: Validates the victim's pain with empathy.

rubric.point: Publicly correct the false rumor in front of the same peer group where it was spoken
rubric.note: Makes active public restitution to restore dignity.

dangerous: say 'it was just a joke bro'
blame the classmate who originally started the rumor

sources.name: CBSE School Counseling Guidelines - Restorative Practices

cards.title: Coping with exclusion: You are not defined by someone's clique
facts: Social exclusion activates the same anterior cingulate cortex pain pathways in the brain as physical bodily injury.
Being excluded by a school clique is usually about group insecurity and conformity, not an indictment of your worth as a person.
do: Remind yourself: 'Their choice to exclude me reflects their group dynamics, not my value as a human'
Direct your energy toward cultivating one or two authentic, kind individual friendships rather than chasing popular cliques
Engage in passion-driven clubs (music, robotics, sports, art) where connection forms around shared interests
dont: Never change your core ethical values or mock others just to win acceptance from an exclusive clique
Never isolate yourself entirely or conclude that nobody in the world will ever like you

myths.statement: If a popular group of classmates doesn't invite you to sit at their table, it proves you are inherently unlikable.
myths.truth: Clique behavior thrives on artificial exclusion to manufacture status. Your worth is completely independent of their group dynamics.

quiz.q: When dealing with painful social exclusion at school, what is the most constructive response?
options: Beg them to let you hang out with them
Seek out genuine shared-interest clubs and invest in individual friendships based on mutual kindness
Spread hateful gossip about everyone in the clique
Stop eating lunch entirely
quiz.explanation: Focusing on genuine shared interests and quality individual relationships builds lasting social resilience.

situations: At lunch break at {at}, {name} sees classmates whispering and laughing while hiding their phones, deliberately leaving {name} out of an outing.
scenario.question: How should {name} navigate this painful moment?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Acknowledge the sting of exclusion without internalizing it as a personal defect
rubric.note: Practices emotional regulation and self-worth protection.
rubric.keys: acknowledge pain|do not internalize defect|protect self worth

rubric.point: Step away from the clique and sit with someone else or join a library activity
rubric.note: Chooses healthy social alternatives over begging for inclusion.
rubric.keys: step away from clique|find kind peers|join library group

rubric.point: Talk through the feelings with a trusted sibling, parent, or school counselor
rubric.note: Processes social distress with supportive adults.

dangerous: plead with the group to accept you

sources.name: National Mental Health Programme - Adolescent Life Skills

cards.title: Being there for a friend: Compassionate listening over quick fixes
facts: When friends are in deep sorrow or distress, they don't need cliches like 'everything happens for a reason'; they need non-judgmental presence.
Distinguish everyday teenage sadness from mental health crises; never promise to keep secrets about self-harm or suicide.
do: Sit with them, listen actively, and say: 'I hear how heavy this feels for you; you are not alone'
Offer practical micro-support: walking together, sharing class notes, or getting a glass of water
If a friend mentions self-harm, hopelessness, or giving up on life, tell a trusted adult immediately
dont: Never dismiss their pain with toxic positivity like 'just smile and cheer up!'
NEVER promise to keep a secret when a friend's physical life or safety is at risk

myths.statement: If a distressed friend asks you to promise never to tell anyone about their self-harm plans, you must keep that secret no matter what.
myths.truth: Life safety overrides all secrecy promises. True friendship means breaking confidence to save a friend's life by notifying adults.

quiz.q: What is the most supportive thing to say when a friend breaks down crying over family troubles?
options: 'Stop crying, it's not a big deal'
'I am here with you, take all the time you need, and I'm listening'
'My problems are way worse than yours'
'You should just smile more'
quiz.explanation: Validating presence and active listening provide safety and comfort without judgment or unsolicited advice.

situations: Sitting on the bench at {at}, a close friend confides that they feel hopeless, overwhelmed by family conflict, and want to end their pain.
scenario.question: How should {name} respond with care and responsibility?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Listen with deep empathy and stay physically present with the friend
rubric.keys: deep empathy|stay present|do not leave alone

rubric.point: Clearly explain that you care about their life too much to keep thoughts of harm a secret
rubric.keys: refuse to keep self harm secret|care too much

rubric.point: Guide the friend directly to the school counselor or call the Tele-MANAS helpline 14416 together
rubric.note: Connects crisis situation with professional mental health care.

dangerous: promise to keep suicidal thoughts secret
leave friend alone in isolated spot

sources.name: Tele-MANAS Toll Free 24/7 Mental Health Helpline (14416)

cards.title: Cooling the fire: Managing anger before saying things you regret
facts: Anger is a secondary emotion that usually masks underlying hurt, fear, frustration, or perceived injustice.
When angry, your brain releases adrenaline that impairs logical judgment; taking a mandatory cooling break prevents catastrophic blowups.
do: Recognize physical anger cues: clenched fists, racing pulse, hot neck, or shallow breathing
Enforce the 10-second rule: count slowly from 1 to 10 or drink a cold glass of water before replying
Step away physically: 'I am too angry to talk fairly right now; I will talk when I cool down'
dont: Never send text messages, post online comments, or make major decisions while enraged
Never resort to physical aggression, breaking items, or screaming insults

myths.statement: Venting anger by punching walls, screaming, and smashing plates helps you get rid of anger safely.
myths.truth: Research shows physical aggressive venting rehearses and amplifies anger pathways. Slow breathing and physical stepping away extinguish it.

quiz.q: What physiological action is scientifically proven to de-escalate acute anger rapidly?
options: Screaming at the top of your lungs into a pillow
Slow diaphragmatic exhalations and physical cold water face washing
Punching a door
Writing an angry email immediately
quiz.explanation: Slow exhalations trigger the vagus nerve and parasympathetic system, reducing heart rate and blood pressure.

situations: During a heated football dispute on the playground at {at}, an opponent shoves {name} and insults {name}'s family.
scenario.question: How should {name} handle the surge of intense anger?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Step back, take deep diaphragmatic breaths, and refuse to engage in physical violence
rubric.note: De-escalates physical conflict through emotional discipline.

rubric.point: Tell the referee or sports teacher clearly about the foul play rather than retaliating
rubric.note: Uses official grievance systems over street fighting.
rubric.keys: report to referee or teacher|do not retaliate

rubric.point: Allow bodily adrenaline to subside before discussing the dispute with the opponent
rubric.keys: let adrenaline subside|cool down before talking

dangerous: punch the opponent in the face

cards.title: The comparison trap: Highlight reels vs real life
facts: Comparing your messy behind-the-scenes life to other people's curated, filtered social media highlight reels creates chronic depression and envy.
Social media algorithms intentionally amplify envy and luxury flexes because outrage and desire drive longer screen time.
do: Remind yourself: 'Nobody posts their failed exams, family fights, or morning acne on Instagram'
Mute or unfollow accounts that consistently leave you feeling inadequate, ugly, or poor
Spend time celebrating your real-world achievements: books read, sports played, and genuine friendships
dont: Never measure your beauty or worth by the number of likes, hearts, or views on a photo
Never buy items you cannot afford just to photograph them for social media clout

myths.statement: People whose social media profiles show luxury vacations, flawless skin, and constant parties live genuinely perfect lives.
myths.truth: Social feeds are carefully curated stage performances. Influencers often experience severe anxiety, loneliness, and financial strain behind the camera.

quiz.q: Why does scrolling through luxury vacation photos on social media frequently make teenagers feel depressed?
options: Because phones emit radiation that causes sadness
Because you are comparing your unfiltered everyday reality to someone else's top 1% staged highlight reel
Because vacations are bad for health
Because phones are too heavy
quiz.explanation: Comparing your private struggles to another person's public best moments creates an artificial, toxic illusion of personal deficiency.

situations: Late at night in bed at {at}, {name} scrolls through classmates' beach holiday stories and feels a deep ache of inadequacy and sadness.
scenario.question: What is the healthiest mental shift for {name}?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Recognize that social media stories are selective highlights and turn off the device
rubric.note: Breaks the comparison spiral through reality testing.
rubric.keys: recognize selective highlights|turn off phone|stop scrolling

rubric.point: Unfollow or mute accounts that trigger persistent feelings of envy and inadequacy
Write down three specific blessings or accomplishments in your own everyday life

dangerous: stay up all night stewing in jealousy
beg parents to take out loans for luxury trips
post fake staged photos to compete

sources.name: UNICEF - Digital Parenting and Mental Health

cards.title: Disagreeing with grace: Attack the argument, not the person
facts: Two smart, kind people can look at the same facts and come to completely different conclusions; disagreement is normal in society.
Attacking a person's intelligence, character, or family (ad hominem) destroys dialogue; focusing on evidence builds shared wisdom.
do: Listen to understand the other person's perspective rather than listening merely to formulate your counter-attack
Use phrases like: 'I see your point about X, but what about the evidence on Y?'
Separate someone's ideas from their character: you can reject an idea while fully respecting the human holding it
dont: Never resort to name-calling, sarcastic mocking, or shouting over someone to win a debate
Never turn an intellectual or political difference into a lifelong personal grudge

myths.statement: If you truly believe you are right in a debate, it is fully justified to insult the other person's intelligence.
myths.truth: Insults are the weapon of someone who has run out of solid reasoning. Respectful logic and evidence persuade; personal attacks alienate.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a constructive debate from a destructive argument?
options: Using louder vocal volume than your opponent
Focusing on facts and logic while treating the other person with dignity and respect
Insulting their family background
Interrupting them every two seconds
quiz.explanation: Constructive debate examines evidence objectively without degrading human relationships.

situations: In the school debate club at {at}, an opponent presents an argument that {name} strongly disagrees with.
scenario.question: How should {name} structure the rebuttal?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Acknowledge the opponent's core premise respectfully before presenting counter-evidence
rubric.note: Practices intellectual charity and respectful debate.

rubric.point: Address the factual data and reasoning directly without mocking the opponent personally
rubric.keys: address data and reasoning|no personal insults

rubric.point: Keep tone calm and modulated to allow the merits of the argument to speak for themselves

dangerous: refuse to shake hands after debate

sources.name: National Curriculum Framework - Life Skills & Critical Thinking

cards.title: Building your safety circle: Identifying trusted adults
facts: Every young person encounters problems too heavy to carry alone—bullying, family distress, abuse, or deep depression.
A trusted adult is someone who listens without mocking, protects your physical safety, respects boundaries, and takes constructive action.
do: Identify at least 3 trusted adults in different settings: one at home, one at school (teacher/counselor), and one in the community (doctor/relative)
Practice reaching out: 'I am dealing with something really difficult and I need your guidance'
Save national safety helpline numbers (Childline 1098, Tele-MANAS 14416) in your contacts
dont: Never suffer in silent isolation believing that nobody cares or that you deserve to suffer
Never trust an adult who demands that you keep dark, abusive, or uncomfortable physical secrets

myths.statement: Going to a teacher or counselor for help with heavy emotional problems is a sign of personal weakness.
myths.truth: Asking for help when overwhelmed is the highest form of courage and wisdom. No human is equipped to solve every crisis alone.

quiz.q: Which of the following qualities indicates an adult is genuinely trustworthy to confide in?
options: They ask you to keep secret meetings hidden from your parents
They listen patiently without mockery, respect your dignity, and prioritize your safety
They gossip about other students' problems
They dismiss your feelings as stupid
quiz.explanation: Trustworthy adults maintain safety, active listening, healthy boundaries, and mature responsibility.

situations: Facing overwhelming anxiety and family conflict at home at {at}, {name} feels trapped and doesn't know who to turn to.
scenario.question: How should {name} seek appropriate support?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Reach out to a trusted school counselor, favorite teacher, or school nurse during recess
rubric.keys: reach out to counselor|trusted teacher|school nurse

rubric.point: State clearly: 'I am feeling overwhelmed and need help finding a safe way forward'
Know that if school adults are unavailable, national helplines like Tele-MANAS (14416) offer free support

dangerous: turn to unverified strangers on internet chat rooms

sources.name: Childline India 1098 - Ministry of Women and Child Development

cards.title: Starting fresh: Navigating a new school or city transition
facts: Relocating to a new school or city triggers culture shock, grief for old friendships, and feelings of social disorientation.
It takes an average of 3 to 6 months for a new environment to feel familiar; early loneliness is completely normal and temporary.
do: Give yourself permission to feel awkward; transitioning into new routines takes time
Take initiative with low-pressure moves: smile, ask for directions, or offer to carry sports equipment
Join at least one co-curricular club (choir, chess, sports, art) to connect over structured activities
dont: Never isolate yourself in corners with headphones on during every recess break
Never compare the new school unfavorably in front of new classmates ('my old city was 100x better')

myths.statement: If you don't make three best friends on your very first day at a new school, you will be an outcast forever.
myths.truth: Deep friendships take months of repeated proximity and shared experiences to develop. Give yourself time to settle in.

quiz.q: What is the single most effective way to begin making friends when transferring to a new school?
options: Bragging about how much cooler your old school was
Joining a school club or sports team where students collaborate around a shared activity
Sitting alone with a hoodie over your eyes
Insulting the teachers
quiz.explanation: Co-curricular clubs provide structured shared tasks where casual conversations spark friendships naturally.

situations: On their first week at a new school in a new city at {at}, {name} sits alone in the cafeteria feeling deeply homesick and awkward.
scenario.question: How should {name} navigate this transition?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Recognize that early loneliness is a universal transition phase that eases over months
rubric.keys: transition takes time|homesick is normal|be patient

rubric.point: Sign up for a sports team, science club, or drama group to meet peers naturally
rubric.keys: join sports or club|meet peers naturally

rubric.point: Ask a classmate a simple question about school homework or cafeteria menus to break the ice

dangerous: complain loudly that the new city is terrible

sources.name: NCERT Guidelines on Guidance & Counseling for School Students

cards.title: Grief and loss: Walking through bereavement with patience
facts: Losing a beloved grandparent, parent, sibling, or pet triggers waves of sorrow, numbness, anger, and deep yearning.
Grief does not follow a neat straight line; it comes in unpredictable waves that gradually become more manageable over time.
do: Allow yourself to cry and express sorrow without feeling embarrassed or weak
Create a memory box, photo album, or journal preserving fond memories and lessons from your loved one
Maintain basic physical routines: eat regular meals, drink water, and get fresh air even when sad
dont: Never tell yourself 'I should be over this by now'; there is no statutory timeline for grief
Never bottle up painful emotions or pretend you don't care to look 'tough'

myths.statement: Properly grieving means crying for exactly one week, after which you should never feel sad about the person again.
myths.truth: Grief comes in waves over years. You never 'get over' losing someone deeply loved; you learn to grow around the loss.

quiz.q: What is the healthiest mindset when dealing with the painful loss of a loved one or family pet?
options: Force yourself to never mention their name again
Allow feelings of sadness to surface without shame, while leaning on family support and fond memories
Blame yourself for their death
Lock yourself in a dark room for a year
quiz.explanation: Patience, gentle self-care, and shared remembrance allow the heart to heal without suppression.

situations: Following the passing of a beloved grandparent at {at}, {name} feels sudden bursts of tears during class and struggles to concentrate on schoolwork.
scenario.question: How should {name} handle this season of bereavement?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Allow the tears to flow and explain to a kind teacher that you are currently grieving a family loss
rubric.keys: allow tears|tell teacher about loss|express sorrow

rubric.point: Share memories and feelings openly with family members rather than isolating in secret
Engage in a quiet reflective remembrance like planting a tree or creating a memory scrapbook

sources.name: NIMHANS Bereavement and Grief Support Resources

cards.title: The power of 'YET': Transforming fear of failure into growth
facts: Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck demonstrated that a 'Fixed Mindset' views ability as static, while a 'Growth Mindset' views intelligence as a muscle.
Adding the word 'YET' ('I don't understand quadratic equations YET') rewires the brain from defeat into constructive learning mode.
do: Replace 'I can't do this' with 'I haven't mastered this yet'
Treat mistakes as diagnostic data showing exactly where your understanding needs reinforcement
Focus praise and self-talk on effort, strategy, and perseverance rather than innate 'genius'
dont: Never avoid challenging subjects or sports competitions purely out of fear of looking foolish
Never attach your core human worth to an exam score or competition rank

myths.statement: If you fail a mathematics test, it proves that your brain simply lacks the innate DNA for math.
myths.truth: The brain possesses neuroplasticity; struggling through hard problems literally builds new neural synapses and mathematical ability.

quiz.q: What simple three-letter word transforms a defeatist statement into an empowering growth mindset?
options: NOT
YET
WHY
NOW
quiz.explanation: 'Yet' acknowledges current challenge while emphasizing that mastery develops through practice over time.

situations: After scoring 35% on a class physics test at {at}, {name} throws down the paper declaring: 'I am terrible at physics, I give up.'
scenario.question: How can {name} reframe this setback with a growth mindset?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Reframe the thought: 'I don't understand these mechanics concepts YET, but I can improve with practice'
rubric.note: Applies the neuroplastic growth mindset filter.
rubric.keys: power of yet|not understood yet|effort and practice

rubric.point: Review the marked paper to identify specific concept gaps and error patterns
rubric.note: Uses test as diagnostic learning data.

rubric.point: Seek targeted help from a teacher or peer to practice 5 similar problem types

sources.name: Mindset Works - Dr. Carol Dweck Research Foundation

cards.title: Rewiring the negativity bias: The 3 Good Things exercise
facts: The human brain evolved a natural 'negativity bias' that magnifies threats and forgets everyday blessings and safety.
Spending 2 minutes writing down '3 Good Things' every evening physically rewires neural pathways, boosting optimism and sleep quality.
do: Write down 3 specific things that went well today before going to bed, no matter how small
Note why each good thing happened ('I had a warm samosa because Mom thought of me')
Express spontaneous verbal appreciation to people who help you (parents, conductors, sweepers)
dont: Never dismiss small joys (a cool breeze, a funny joke) as trivial or unworthy of gratitude
Never use gratitude to toxicly invalidate genuine pain; gratitude complements problem solving

myths.statement: Practicing gratitude means pretending that bad things never happen and ignoring all life problems.
myths.truth: Gratitude doesn't ignore hardship; it balances brain chemistry so you don't overlook daily goodness while solving life challenges.

quiz.q: What is the proven neurological benefit of writing down 3 good things each evening?
options: It makes you forget everything you learned
It counteracts evolutionary negativity bias and strengthens positive neural pathways
It makes you sleep 18 hours straight
It cures all viral infections
quiz.explanation: Systematic gratitude practice trains the brain to notice resources, kindness, and beauty rather than only threats.

situations: At the end of a tiring, stressful school day at {at}, {name} feels drained, grumpy, and convinced that the whole day was a disaster.
scenario.question: How can {name} reset their mental state before sleeping?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Spend 3 minutes noting three concrete things that were positive during the day
rubric.keys: three good things|concrete positive moments|evening reset

rubric.point: Reflect on the simple daily privileges often taken for granted: clean drinking water, a comfortable bed, family presence
Notice how this gentle practice reduces nighttime anxiety and tension

dangerous: scroll angry comments on social media before bed

sources.name: Greater Good Science Center - UC Berkeley Gratitude Studies

cards.title: Body neutrality: Valuing what your body DOES over how it LOOKS
facts: Commercial advertising, cinema, and social media airbrushing create impossible beauty standards that trigger body dysmorphia.
Body neutrality moves beyond forced praise: instead of obsessing over whether your body is 'pretty', appreciate what your body enables you to DO.
do: Thank your legs for running, your lungs for breathing, and your hands for drawing or playing music
Remember that fashion models and celebrities use heavy makeup, professional lighting, and AI filters
Wear comfortable clothing that fits your current body comfortably rather than squeezing into painful sizes
dont: Never skip meals or adopt extreme starvation diets to look like an internet influencer
Never make unsolicited comments on someone else's weight, skin shade, height, or facial features

myths.statement: Having visible acne, stretch marks, body hair, or skin pores is a medical defect that means you are dirty.
myths.truth: Pores, textures, and body hair are universal biological traits. Airbrushed social media pictures erase normal human biology with digital software.

quiz.q: What is the core philosophy of 'Body Neutrality'?
options: Constantly staring in the mirror reciting that you are the most gorgeous person alive
Appreciating your body as an incredible instrument for living, learning, and feeling rather than an ornament for display
Ignoring your body's need for food and water
Wearing plastic bags to hide yourself
quiz.explanation: Body neutrality frees young people from appearance obsession by focusing on functional health and capability.

situations: Looking in the mirror at {at}, {name} feels miserable about emerging facial acne and wants to skip a school presentation.
scenario.question: How should {name} reframe this self-conscious moment?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Recognize that adolescent acne is a natural hormonal phase experienced by nearly all teenagers

cards.title: Exiting group chat drama: Preserving peace over flame wars
facts: Class WhatsApp and Discord groups frequently devolve into late-night gossip, meme mocking, exclusion, and aggressive flame wars.
Getting drawn into typing frantic counter-attacks late at night drains emotional energy and creates permanent screenshot evidence.
do: Mute high-drama group chats for 8 hours or 1 year so notifications do not disrupt your peace
Step back and ask: 'Will this argument matter in 1 month? Is typing a reply making anyone kinder?'
Exit toxic group chats cleanly or speak to the group admin privately about basic civility rules
dont: Never forward cruel memes or screenshots targeting a classmate to other chat groups
Never post personal secrets or intimate feelings into large peer group chats

myths.statement: If someone insults you in a class group chat, you must immediately insult them back with ten memes to protect your honor.
myths.truth: Escalating flame wars gives trolls exactly the spectacle they desire. Muting, documenting violations, or walking away displays true strength.

quiz.q: What is the most mature response when a class WhatsApp group erupts into malicious bullying against a classmate?
options: Add funny laughing emojis to stay on the bullies' good side
Refuse to participate in the mockery, support the targeted classmate privately, and report the abuse to a teacher
Forward the screenshots to 20 other groups
Insult everyone's parents
quiz.explanation: Refusing complicity, offering private empathy to the victim, and alerting adults stops bullying cycles without feeding drama.

rubric.point: Resist the urge to jump into the late-night flame war and mute the group chat notifications

Put the phone in another room to protect sleep and report severe cyberbullying to school tomorrow
rubric.note: Safeguards rest and utilizes institutional safety channels.
rubric.keys: put phone away|sleep peacefully|report severe abuse

cards.title: Talking to parents: Bridging the mental health conversation gap
facts: Many traditional parents dismiss emotional distress as 'just laziness' or 'too much mobile phone' because they grew up without mental health language.
Approaching parents with vulnerability, specific symptoms, and patience bridges generational divides far better than angry shouting.
do: Choose a calm, quiet moment when parents are not stressed from work or chores to initiate the conversation
Use 'I-statements': 'Mom/Dad, I have been feeling constantly exhausted and anxious for three weeks, and I need guidance'
Frame mental health like physical health: 'Just like we see a doctor for high fever, I think speaking to a counselor would help me'
dont: Never begin a sensitive emotional conversation during the middle of a screaming argument
Never dismiss parents as unloving simply because they initially struggle to understand clinical depression

myths.statement: If parents say 'just do yoga and study harder', it proves they completely hate you and you can never talk to them.
myths.truth: Parents often respond with yoga/study out of genuine care filtered through limited past knowledge. Patient education bridges the gap.

quiz.q: How should you phrase a request to see a counselor when speaking to traditional parents?
options: 'You ruined my life and I hate this house!'
'I have been struggling with persistent anxiety that is affecting my studies and sleep; could we consult a counselor together?'
'Give me 50,000 rupees for therapy right now'
'I am never taking another exam'
quiz.explanation: Connecting emotional support to physical health, academic performance, and mutual partnership reassures parents and unlocks support.

rubric.note: Anchors distress in tangible, relatable symptoms.

rubric.note: Provides low-barrier, reassuring professional entry point.

cards.title: Sleep and emotional stability: Your brain's nightly wash cycle
facts: During deep REM and slow-wave sleep, the brain's glymphatic system cleans out toxic metabolic waste and emotionally recalibrates the amygdala.
Chronic sleep deprivation of under 7 hours produces emotional volatility, irritability, and depressive symptoms identical to clinical mood disorders.
do: Aim for 8 to 9 hours of uninterrupted sleep every night as a non-negotiable mental health foundation
Keep bedroom dark and cool, and stop looking at blue-light screens at least 45 minutes before sleep
Maintain consistent sleep and wake times even on weekends to synchronize your circadian rhythm
dont: Never sacrifice sleep as a badge of honor to prove how hard you study
Never consume caffeinated energy drinks or coffee in the late afternoon or evening

myths.statement: Sleeping only 4 hours a night is a sign of high ambition and supreme mental discipline.
myths.truth: Chronic sleep deprivation damages IQ, destroys working memory, impairs emotional control, and triggers long-term mental health breakdowns.

quiz.q: What happens to your emotional regulation centers when you are severely sleep-deprived?
options: They become 10 times stronger and calmer
The emotional amygdala becomes hyper-reactive while the prefrontal logical control center disconnects
You become immune to sadness
Nothing changes
quiz.explanation: Sleep deprivation uncouples prefrontal regulatory control, making you prone to sudden crying, rage, and anxiety.
